Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) -- A Zimbabwe High Court judge is trying to take the country's first lady to court, accusing her of using political muscle to wrest from him a farm he was given during the land seizures. Judge says Grace Mugabe, pictured with her husband, effectively took his farm by force. The matter has not been given a date, however, amid reports that other judges have been refusing to hear it. High Court Judge Ben Hlatshwayo is suing a company owned by Grace Mugabe, wife of President Robert Mugabe, for grabbing Gwina Farm in Banket, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) northwest of Harare. The farm is near Mugabe's rural home. The judge said he acquired the farm in December 2002 as part of President Mugabe's controversial land grabs, in which Mugabe took land from white commercial farmers and distributed it to black Zimbabweans. In an affidavit, filed at the High Court in Harare, the judge said the "unlawful conduct" by Grace Mugabe's company, Gushungo Holdings, amounted to spoilation -- or taking of the farm by force. He said emissaries of the first lady have been visiting the farm frequently and issuing instructions to workers, according to court documents. "There is clearly no lawful basis for such interference, which conduct, by its very nature, amounts to spoliation," Hlatshwayo wrote in the papers. Lands and Resettlement Minister Didymus Mutasa said the judge had been given alternative land as compensation for the farm that Grace Mugabe wants to have. Mutasa opposes the judge's affidavit. Hlatshwayo said he had been operating his farm in "quiet, undisturbed, peaceful possession, occupation and production" since it was allocated to him. Since the land grabs, Zimbabwe has been facing acute shortages of food that critics say is a result of Mugabe giving the land to inexperienced peasant farmers. But Mugabe blames the West for the shortages, saying Western countries are sabotaging him after he took the land for his people. Mugabe says the land reform was meant to reverse colonial imbalances remaining after British rule. The legal wrangle comes after Grace Mugabe was accused of assaulting a journalist in Hong Kong who wanted to take photos of her while she was on a shopping spree. Lawmakers were supposed to debate a bill next week for a constitutional amendment that would create the new posts called for under the deal, including the post of prime minister for opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai. The delay could prolong the country's political and economic crisis. The delay comes a day after the MDC accused Mugabe's ZANU-PF of backtracking on the implementation of a power-sharing deal the party signed with Tsvangirai in September. Tsvangirai agreed last week to join the unity government if "outstanding issues" were addressed. While government officials could not be reached for comment, Zimbabwean Justice Minister Patrick Chinamasa was quoted by the state media as saying the delay in debate on the constitutional-amendment bill would push back next week's deadline. A coalition government is seen by many as a panacea to halt the meltdown of Zimbabwe's economy. The country is also facing its worst humanitarian crisis, with acute shortages of all essentials such as fuel, food, electricity and public-health delivery system. A ravaging cholera outbreak has affected 65,000 people and claimed close to 3,500 lives since its outbreak in August.

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) — A Zimbabwean High Court judge is seeking legal action against the country’s first lady, alleging that she used her political influence to forcibly take over a farm allocated to him during the government’s land-seizure program.

No hearing date has been scheduled, reportedly because other judges have declined to consider the case.

High Court Judge Ben Hlatshwayo has filed suit against Gushungo Holdings, a company owned by Grace Mugabe, the wife of President Robert Mugabe. He accuses the company of taking control of Gwina Farm in Banket, roughly 100 kilometers (62 miles) northwest of Harare and close to Mugabe’s rural residence.

Hlatshwayo said the property was assigned to him in December 2002 under President Mugabe’s controversial land-redistribution campaign. During that program, farms were taken from white commercial farmers and handed to black Zimbabweans.

In an affidavit submitted to the High Court in Harare, Hlatshwayo described Gushungo Holdings’ actions as unlawful and said they constituted “spoliation,” meaning the farm was effectively seized by force. Court documents state that representatives of the first lady repeatedly visited the property and gave orders to farm employees.

Hlatshwayo wrote that there was “clearly no lawful basis” for the interference and that the conduct, by its nature, amounted to spoliation.

Lands and Resettlement Minister Didymus Mutasa disputes the judge’s affidavit. He said Hlatshwayo had been offered another piece of land as compensation for the farm Grace Mugabe wanted.

The judge maintained that, from the time the farm was allocated to him, he had possessed, occupied and operated it quietly, peacefully and without disruption.

Zimbabwe has experienced severe food shortages since the land seizures. Critics attribute the crisis to Mugabe’s decision to transfer farms to inexperienced peasant farmers. Mugabe, however, blames Western nations, accusing them of undermining his government because he reclaimed the land for Zimbabweans. He has said the reforms were intended to correct colonial-era inequalities that remained after British rule.

The farm dispute follows accusations that Grace Mugabe assaulted a journalist in Hong Kong who attempted to photograph her during a shopping trip.

Separately, lawmakers had been expected the following week to consider a constitutional-amendment bill establishing new government positions required under a political agreement, including a prime minister’s post for opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai. A postponement could extend Zimbabwe’s political and economic turmoil.

The delay was announced one day after the Movement for Democratic Change accused Mugabe’s ZANU-PF party of retreating from the power-sharing agreement it signed with Tsvangirai in September. Tsvangirai had agreed the previous week to enter a unity government, provided that unresolved matters were settled.

Government representatives were unavailable for comment. However, state media quoted Justice Minister Patrick Chinamasa as saying that postponing debate on the constitutional amendment would also move back the deadline set for the following week.

Many regard a coalition government as the best way to stop Zimbabwe’s economic collapse. The country is also enduring its most serious humanitarian emergency, marked by critical shortages of essentials including fuel, food and electricity, as well as the breakdown of public-health services.

A devastating cholera epidemic had infected 65,000 people and killed nearly 3,500 since beginning in August.

Hlatshwayo said he had received the property under Zimbabwe’s controversial land redistribution program but was later displaced through the use of political influence, intimidation, and force. The claims were allegations before the court and required judicial determination.

The dispute was especially significant because Hlatshwayo himself had benefited from the land-reform system established by President Robert Mugabe’s government. Beginning in 2000, that program transferred thousands of mostly white-owned commercial farms to Black Zimbabweans, officially to correct colonial-era inequalities in land ownership. In practice, critics argued that the process was frequently violent, poorly administered, and vulnerable to manipulation by politically connected officials and members of the ruling elite.

By challenging a business linked to Grace Mugabe, Hlatshwayo’s case exposed tensions within the system that had overseen those transfers. His lawsuit suggested that even recipients holding land under government authority could lose it when confronted by individuals with greater political power. It also raised broader concerns about judicial independence and whether Zimbabwe’s courts could provide an effective remedy in a dispute involving the president’s family.

The controversy formed part of the wider economic and legal aftermath of Zimbabwe’s land seizures. The rapid disruption of commercial agriculture, combined with drought, shortages of financing and farm inputs, and broader economic mismanagement, contributed to falling production, unemployment, and recurring food shortages. Disputes over ownership and occupancy also created prolonged uncertainty for farmers and investors.

Hlatshwayo’s lawsuit therefore concerned more than control of a single farm. It became an example of alleged abuse of state power under the Mugabe government and of the instability created when land rights depended heavily on political patronage. The case underscored the continuing challenge Zimbabwe faced in addressing historical inequality while establishing secure property rights, accountable government, and a productive agricultural sector.

Judge Ben Hlatshwayo says Gushungo Holdings took control of Gwina Farm, near the farming town of Banket, despite his claim to the property. In court papers, Hlatshwayo is seeking to have the company removed from the land and his rights to the farm recognized.

The power-sharing administration brought together Mugabe’s ZANU-PF and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai’s Movement for Democratic Change after disputed elections and widespread violence in 2008.

It also follows a devastating cholera epidemic linked to the collapse of water, sanitation and public-health systems. The outbreak infected tens of thousands of people and killed more than 4,000, according to international health agencies.

counterfactuals.output:
**Grace Mugabe accused of taking over judge’s farm as Zimbabwe’s land disputes persist**

**HARARE** — Zimbabwe’s former first lady Grace Mugabe has been accused of unlawfully taking control of a farm near Harare, in a dispute that has returned the country’s contentious land politics and concerns over elite privilege to the courts.

In an application filed with Zimbabwe’s High Court, the farm’s occupants allege that Mugabe, the widow of longtime president Robert Mugabe, or people acting on her behalf entered the property and displaced those in possession without obtaining a court order. They are seeking relief under the legal remedy known as *spoliation*.

The allegations have not been tested in court. Mugabe’s response was not immediately available, and the proceedings do not in themselves determine who legally owns the property.

Under Zimbabwean law, which draws heavily on Roman-Dutch legal principles, a spoliation application is intended to restore the position that existed before someone was forcibly or unlawfully deprived of property. To succeed, an applicant generally must show that they were in peaceful and undisturbed possession and that this possession was taken away without consent or lawful process.

Crucially, the court does not initially decide ownership. The principle behind the remedy — often expressed as “no one may take the law into their own hands” — requires possession to be restored first, leaving competing claims to title or occupation to be resolved separately.

The case is politically sensitive because it involves both the family of Zimbabwe’s former ruler and a member of the judiciary. It also echoes longstanding complaints that politically connected figures have been able to acquire or occupy land despite court challenges and competing claims.

Robert Mugabe’s government launched a fast-track land redistribution programme in 2000, seizing thousands of mostly white-owned commercial farms. The policy was promoted as a correction to colonial-era dispossession, but its implementation was frequently violent and chaotic. Critics said multiple farms were allocated to senior officials while some experienced agricultural workers were driven off the land.

The upheaval contributed to a steep fall in commercial farming output, although drought, sanctions, limited access to finance and wider policy failures also played roles in Zimbabwe’s prolonged economic decline.

Mugabe was removed in a military intervention in 2017 and replaced by his former deputy, Emmerson Mnangagwa. Mnangagwa promised to restore the rule of law, attract investment and compensate dispossessed farmers, but Zimbabwe continues to struggle with high prices, currency instability, unemployment and chronic shortages of public services.

The government has introduced successive currencies in an attempt to end the country’s dependence on the US dollar and restrain inflation. Public confidence, however, has remained fragile, while businesses and households continue to rely heavily on foreign currency.

Zimbabwe’s political divisions have also deepened following disputed elections and repeated arrests of opposition activists. Rights groups accuse the authorities of using the police, courts and restrictive legislation to suppress dissent. The government denies acting politically and says it is enforcing the law and protecting national stability.

Against that backdrop, the farm case is likely to be watched as a test of whether Zimbabwe’s courts can enforce due process in a dispute involving a powerful political family.

A ruling in favour of spoliation would not establish final ownership of the land. It would mean only that the previous occupants must be restored to possession until the underlying rights are determined through lawful proceedings.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you provide a detailed report about the Zimbabwean judge who accused First Lady Grace Mugabe of using her political influence to seize his farm?
counterfactuals.output:
## Report: Justice Ben Hlatshwayo’s farm dispute with Grace Mugabe

The judge was **Justice Ben Hlatshwayo**, then a senior Zimbabwean High Court judge who later served on the Supreme Court. In the late 2000s, Hlatshwayo alleged that **First Lady Grace Mugabe used her position and access to state officials to try to take over a farm allocated to him under Zimbabwe’s land-reform programme**.

### The property at the centre of the dispute

The dispute concerned **Gwina Farm**, in the Banket area of Mashonaland West Province, northwest of Harare. Hlatshwayo had received the property from the government during Zimbabwe’s fast-track land redistribution programme, which began in 2000 and transferred thousands of predominantly white-owned commercial farms to Black Zimbabweans.

Reports at the time described Hlatshwayo as having invested in the farm and treated himself as its lawful state-approved occupier. As with most redistributed land, however, the state retained ultimate control over the property, normally through an “offer letter” or lease rather than unrestricted freehold title. This left beneficiaries vulnerable to having their allocations withdrawn or reassigned.

### Hlatshwayo’s accusation

According to court papers and contemporary news reports, Hlatshwayo maintained that Grace Mugabe wanted Gwina Farm and had used her political standing to influence land-administration officials. His case was essentially that:

- his official allocation was being cancelled or disregarded;
- the threatened reallocation did not follow an ordinary, transparent administrative process;
- state officials were acting because the intended new beneficiary was the president’s wife; and
- he was being pressured to leave despite having an earlier government entitlement to the land.

The judge reportedly characterized the episode as an exercise of **political influence or “political muscle.”** His complaint was directed principally at the administrative actions of the government and lands authorities, although Grace Mugabe was identified as the person expected to benefit.

The accusation should be understood as **Hlatshwayo’s allegation**, not necessarily as a final judicial finding that Grace Mugabe had personally committed an offence. Reporting on the matter focused on his court filings and the unusually public clash between two members of Zimbabwe’s governing elite.

### Why the case was politically significant

The dispute attracted attention for several reasons.

#### 1. It exposed insecurity within the land-reform system

Even a serving judge and politically connected land-reform beneficiary could apparently face the loss of an allocated property if someone more powerful wanted it. Critics argued that this demonstrated how land allocation had become dependent on political patronage rather than stable rules or secure tenure.

#### 2. It involved a member of the judiciary

Zimbabwe’s judiciary had already faced sustained criticism over political interference, particularly in land cases and disputes involving the ruling party. A judge publicly alleging pressure from the first lady therefore raised broader questions about judicial independence and the ability of courts to restrain executive power.

#### 3. Hlatshwayo was not an opponent of land reform

Hlatshwayo was himself a beneficiary of the redistribution programme and was generally associated with the post-2000 legal and political establishment. The dispute was therefore not a conventional confrontation between the government and a dispossessed white farmer. It was a conflict **within the ruling system over who had the stronger claim to redistributed land**.

This produced a notable irony: a programme that had removed owners and occupiers through state power could also be used to displace one of its own beneficiaries.

#### 4. It reinforced allegations surrounding Grace Mugabe

Grace Mugabe was repeatedly accused by critics of using her proximity to President Robert Mugabe to accumulate land and other assets. She became closely associated with agricultural and property interests around Mazowe, including the Mugabe family’s dairy operations and adjoining estates.

Not every allegation concerning her property holdings was independently proved, and Zimbabwean officials frequently defended such acquisitions as lawful allocations under land reform. Nevertheless, the Hlatshwayo dispute contributed to a broader public image of the first lady as someone able to enlist state institutions in pursuit of private or family interests.

### Broader context

Zimbabwe’s fast-track land reform addressed a genuine historical imbalance created by colonial land dispossession. However, the implementation process was often violent, poorly documented and heavily politicized. Although many ordinary Black farmers received land, senior politicians, military officers, judges and other well-connected figures were also allocated valuable commercial properties.

Because the state could issue, cancel or replace offer letters, competing allocations became common. Courts were often asked to determine whether one beneficiary had a better administrative claim than another, but cases involving the Mugabe family were especially sensitive.

The Hlatshwayo affair illustrated three recurring weaknesses:

1. **uncertain land tenure**, because beneficiaries often lacked permanent title;
2. **overlapping or politically revised allocations**; and
3. **limited institutional protection against intervention by powerful officials**.

### Outcome and evidentiary caution

Public accounts of the dispute are clearer about Hlatshwayo’s allegations than about a definitive final resolution. The matter did not produce a widely reported criminal judgment against Grace Mugabe, nor should it be described as a conclusively proven illegal seizure without qualification.

The most accurate summary is:

> Justice Ben Hlatshwayo alleged in legal proceedings that Grace Mugabe used her exceptional political influence to induce state land authorities to remove or override his rights to Gwina Farm so that she could acquire it.

The episode remains important less because of a clear final verdict than because it showed how Zimbabwe’s land system could become an arena for competition among politically connected elites—and how even a senior judge could claim to be powerless when confronted by the president’s family.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
Zimbabwe’s political and humanitarian crises deepened as Ben Hlatshwayo took legal action against First Lady Grace Mugabe in a dispute over property and land, an unusual public challenge involving Zimbabwe’s ruling family. The case added to scrutiny of elite privilege and the politicization of land and the courts.

At the same time, implementation of the September 2008 power-sharing agreement between President Robert Mugabe’s ZANU-PF and Morgan Tsvangirai’s MDC remained stalled. A constitutional amendment needed to establish the new offices and institutions envisaged by the deal was delayed amid disagreements over its wording and over the allocation of ministries, senior appointments and control of the security apparatus. Although Mugabe and Tsvangirai had agreed in principle to govern together, the failure to resolve those disputes prevented the formation of an effective unity government.

The deadlock was unfolding against an increasingly severe humanitarian emergency. Food shortages left millions dependent on assistance, while hyperinflation, unemployment and the collapse of public services made basic goods and medical care inaccessible to much of the population. A nationwide cholera outbreak, fueled by broken water and sanitation systems, continued to spread, infecting tens of thousands and killing thousands.

Together, the lawsuit, constitutional delay and power-sharing impasse illustrated Zimbabwe’s broader crisis: bitter struggles over political and economic privilege were continuing while hunger, disease and institutional collapse demanded urgent action.
